title: Straight-line ornament: parts, pairs, and possible engines
scope: An authored centre-line reading of all 18 wholly straight-edged rows in three supplied reference sheets. The remaining 10 rows are listed explicitly. These are inspectable construction hypotheses, not recovered drawing histories or automatic image traces.

patterns.name: Running square key
patterns.observed: Short inward hooks repeat between two separate border rails. Their outside reaches advance the band while the hooks turn back into each repeat.
patterns.construction: Build one angular reach word: advance, rise, advance, descend partway, return inward, and descend to the next handoff. Repeat it by translation. Keep the framing rails separate from the ornament course.
alternatives: Place repeated hook cells and connect their exposed ends.
Read alternating upper and lower hooks as two coordinated collections; their handoffs must still be supplied.
patterns.limits: A repeated silhouette does not establish the original pen route. The authored centre-line read ignores printing irregularities and treats border rails as separate participants.

patterns.name: Opposed short hooks
patterns.observed: Shallow hooks alternate between upper and lower portions of the strip. Short returns and longer horizontal reaches give a compact interlocking rhythm.
patterns.construction: Make a short hooked path, place an opposed partner at the next horizontal phase, and repeat the pair. The partnership can be read independently from the top and bottom border rails.
alternatives: Execute one continuous word containing both upper and lower hooks.
Use two translated, vertically opposed streams with an explicit phase relation.
patterns.limits: A vertical reflection alone may not align the two hooks; translation or a different start phase may also be needed. Connectedness belongs to actual handoffs, not close-looking corners.

patterns.name: Key with four-window inserts
patterns.observed: Interleaving angular key routes alternate with small square inserts containing four white windows. The hooked routes have visible crossing sites, and long horizontal rails frame the composition.
patterns.construction: Repeat one ordered key word in two courses separated by half its horizontal repeat. Use a separate placement stream for the square inserts. Construct each insert as an outer square with a vertical and horizontal divider, retaining those material contacts without duplicating the dividers.
alternatives: Repeat a compound group containing both phased key routes and their divided-square inserts.
Drive the key pair and the inserts from separate streams tied to the same repeat surface.
patterns.limits: The chosen through-routing at key crossings is not established by black ink alone. Four white windows do not imply four independent square pens. Exact attachment of inserts to nearby key strokes remains a chosen reconstruction premise.

patterns.name: Broad interlocking angular key
patterns.observed: Long outside reaches surround smaller inward returns. Adjacent key forms interleave and contain visible crossing or contact sites, alongside repeated angular white passages.
patterns.construction: Repeat one angular word in two courses shifted horizontally by half the word's repeat. Its long outer reaches and shorter returns cross the partner at the observed contact sites. Preserve through-routing separately from a connected-junction interpretation.
alternatives: Assemble translated nested-hook cells with explicit end connections.
Describe the white corridor first, then retain its two offset sides as separate material boundaries.
patterns.limits: Coincident contact coordinates do not decide through-routing versus joined flow. The corridor-first description needs a width and side correspondence, and cannot erase those contact sites. Similar hooks do not prove uniform scaling of A1.

patterns.name: In-and-out spiral meander
patterns.observed: The path winds inward through square turns, passes through a short central S-like turnaround, then winds outward between its incoming reaches before advancing to the next coil.
patterns.construction: Repeat a continuous inward-and-outward turn word. Preserve the small central bridge and the outside handoff to the next repeat; they are what distinguish this row from separate finite spiral pens.
alternatives: Construct inward and outward halves as separate exposed paths, then connect them at the central turnaround and the repeat seam.
Read nested square sides with alternating openings that form one inward-and-outward route.
patterns.limits: The earlier coarse survey treated these as finite inward spirals. Closer source inspection shows the central bridge, so that interpretation is superseded here. The continuous path still does not establish a closed loop or an original pen history.

patterns.name: Square medallions and four-hook rosettes
patterns.observed: Large nested-square medallions alternate with groups of four small angular hooks arranged around a center. Several colors distinguish parts in the source.
patterns.construction: Construct two cell types: nested square boundaries, and a quarter-turn orbit of one small hook. Alternate these cells along a shared horizontal repeat. Treat their surrounding border as another participant.
alternatives: Repeat one compound medallion-plus-rosette cell.
Interleave a square-cell stream with a four-hook stream at a shared phase offset.
patterns.limits: This centre-line read intentionally omits color. Nested boundaries do not establish one spiral route. A four-hook arrangement is not automatically one connected four-way junction, and quarter-turn matching must preserve the selected hook roles.

patterns.name: Paired horizontal hooks
patterns.observed: Upper and lower hooked runs oppose one another at staggered positions. A continuous upper rail visibly meets several stems, so this is more than a detached-rail version of A2.
patterns.construction: Repeat the shallow hooks while retaining the continuous upper rail and all stem contacts. Read the contacts as projected incidence first, then select shared-site joins only where the construction explicitly supplies them.
alternatives: Use an alternating upper/lower course together with the observed continuous rail.
Translate two-hook cells beneath a common rail, retaining their exposed stem contacts.
patterns.limits: The source does not supply pen identities or a flow law at rail contacts. A line that looks like a border may already belong to the motif; adding a second copy there creates duplicate material.

patterns.name: Stepped link band
patterns.observed: Small rectangular steps interleave along a narrow strip. Two copies of a step sequence cross at staggered positions.
patterns.construction: Repeat one six-move step word in two courses offset by half a horizontal repeat. Keep the same vertical frame for both copies and preserve their separate through-routing at projected crossings.
alternatives: Translate a bent-cross cell made from separate elbow paths.
Read the repeated small angular openings and reconstruct the surrounding step boundaries.
patterns.limits: Black crossings in this source do not determine over/under or a material junction. The step pairing is an authored explanation; a different grouping can produce the same projected support.

patterns.name: Stacked crosses and diamond openings
patterns.observed: Each separated motif contains two vertically stacked crosses with a diamond-shaped opening between their centers. The motif repeats horizontally between border rails.
patterns.construction: Place four independent diagonal sections as two stacked Xs, retaining their crossings and coincident end contacts. Translate that finite motif with a gap before the next motif rather than connecting everything into a horizontal zigzag lattice.
alternatives: Use two vertically zigging pens with the same projected support, explicitly joining each pen's middle handoff.
Construct the central diamond boundary and its four projecting diagonal arms, preserving the change in native ownership.
patterns.limits: The raster does not distinguish a weld, a crossing, or over/under at the black intersections. Coincident middle endpoints do not select a pen continuation. A diamond only has quarter-turn symmetry when its proportions support that stronger read.

patterns.name: Battlement
patterns.observed: A single stepped course alternates high and low horizontal plateaus between separate horizontal rails.
patterns.construction: Repeat advance, rise, advance, descend. The end of each word is the start of the next. Give the two plateaus and the vertical span shared relations where equality is intended.
alternatives: Repeat U-shaped cells with the required connecting lower spans.
Use a vertical two-state controller alongside a continuing horizontal advance.
patterns.limits: An alternation of levels does not by itself determine plateau widths. The rails are not endpoints of the vertical steps unless the construction explicitly connects them.

patterns.name: Double-depth meander
patterns.observed: Each large rectangular excursion contains a smaller return, producing alternating deep and shallow white passages. Continuous outer rails visibly contact the inner course.
patterns.construction: Extend the battlement word with an inward rectangular return before leaving each large excursion. Repeat the word, then retain the outer rails and their contacts as part of the complete row.
alternatives: Nest a smaller U-like course inside a larger one and connect the appropriate exposed ends.
Compose upper and lower opposed hook groups at a fixed relative phase.
patterns.limits: The standalone inner meander omits observed rail contacts and is only a partial read of this row. Contacts do not specify flow routing. Common nearest clearance does not imply that all white regions have the same width or area.

patterns.name: Stepped courses with detached spots
patterns.observed: Two staggered stepped courses interleave, accompanied by alternating detached spots above and below. The apparent bent-cross motifs emerge where the courses encounter one another.
patterns.construction: Repeat a square-wave word in one course and a second copy shifted both horizontally and vertically. Retain separate spot pens at the alternating free positions. The chosen through-routing keeps both courses continuous through their projected crossings.
alternatives: Cut the same support into coordinated finite elbow pieces, keeping their coincident endpoints distinct until joined.
Repeat a compound group containing both phased step courses and their two spot placements.
patterns.limits: The black crossings do not establish over/under or a material junction. The dots are separate participation, not evidence that a continuous course is interrupted. Other path decompositions can share this projected support.

patterns.name: Compact double-depth meander
patterns.observed: A compact rectilinear course repeats small inward returns within continuous framing. The framing visibly contacts the course at repeated sites.
patterns.construction: Use the nested-return family of B6, choosing a compact repeat. Preserve the ordered handoffs and add the observed framing with its contact correspondence.
alternatives: Repeat one large U with a smaller opposed return inside it.
Compose upper and lower hook collections before selecting a continuous route.
patterns.limits: The inner course alone is a partial read because the framing contacts remain. Similarity to B6 does not prove identical proportions or original construction. The low-resolution reference does not establish exact stroke widths or routing at contacts.

patterns.name: Square-spiral cells
patterns.observed: Finite square coils alternate by a half-turn inside rectangular cell framing. Each coil has a visible inner end and meets its surrounding frame at the outer end.
patterns.construction: Place a finite inward-turn word in one cell, rotate the next copy by a half-turn, and repeat the pair. Retain the surrounding rectangular framing and the coil-to-frame contact correspondence.
alternatives: Repeat a two-cell unit containing one coil and its half-turned partner.
Construct the surrounding cell boundaries first, then attach finite inward paths at alternating sites.
patterns.limits: The inner ends remain finite, unlike the connected turnaround in A5. Frame contacts do not by themselves select a material transfer law. Half-turn placement is different from a vertical reflection, and the coarse source does not establish exact stroke widths.

patterns.name: Diagonal zigzag
patterns.observed: A light zigzag repeatedly rises and falls across a dark band. Each peak and trough joins opposing slopes.
patterns.construction: Repeat one rising diagonal and one falling diagonal while advancing horizontally. Tie their vertical extents when symmetric peaks and troughs are intended.
alternatives: Repeat V-shaped cells and connect their adjacent endpoints.
Combine a steady horizontal stream with a vertically alternating stream.
patterns.limits: The black band is the background in this read, not an additional zigzag strand. Reflection relates slope roles; it does not reverse the order in which the course is traversed.

patterns.name: Dense diagonal mesh
patterns.observed: Several light diagonal strands cross inside a dark strip, leaving a row of small diamond openings and clipped diagonal ends near the strip edges.
patterns.construction: Place two opposed diagonal families with more than one offset lane, then select their support within the strip. Keep clipping separate from a native termination or a turn at the boundary.
alternatives: Repeat a wider multi-crossing cell with explicit continuation ports.
Overlay shifted sparse diamond lattices while retaining their distinct strand identities.
patterns.limits: This is denser than the sparse X band B4. The reference does not identify material junctions or establish over/under. Boundary clipping must not be reported as proof of strand endpoints.

patterns.name: Opposed long meander
patterns.observed: Large upper and lower rectangular reaches contain smaller hooks. Their alternation forms matching angular openings across the band.
patterns.construction: Repeat an ordered meander word containing an upper hooked excursion and an opposed lower excursion. Inspect the two halves separately before reading their combined course.
alternatives: Place a hook and a reflected, shifted partner as a compound repeat.
Construct the alternating white corridors and derive their participating boundary sides.
patterns.limits: Matching the upper and lower halves can require both a reflection and a phase shift. White-region correspondence does not establish that one pen originally traced the whole pattern.

patterns.name: Angular four-strand weave
patterns.observed: Long outer angular strands surround smaller inner runs. Their diagonals interlace near the seams, while separated pair reads reveal large and small hexagon-like openings and diamond-like encounters.
patterns.construction: Use an outer strand word and its vertical reflection, plus a more detailed inner strand word and its reflection. Repeat with the required phase exchange and retain crossing order separately from planar continuation.
alternatives: Treat each reflected pair as one exposed structure, then coordinate the two pair structures.
Use a local encounter construction with continuation, boundary-turn, and complementary over/under laws; the encounter layout would still need evidence.
patterns.limits: Reflected partners share instructions under a change of vertical basis. The outer and inner words are not asserted to be identical at full detail. Selecting a pair exposes useful projected regions but does not by itself discover all white boundaries or recover the historical machine.

excluded.reason: Curved spiral-wave band. Its repeat and rail can be studied separately, but the motif is not a straight-line pattern.
Curved leaf pairs on a stem. The straight stem does not make the full motif eligible for this centre-line polygonal study.
Mixed angular lattice and curved rosette detail. The lattice could be isolated in a later partial read; replacing the curves with corners would invent a different pattern.
Mixed diamond lattice and curved floral centers. The outer lattice is eligible as a component, but the complete row is not wholly straight-edged.
Angular key motifs follow a curved carrier. A local key word is straight-edged, but flattening the whole row would erase the carrier transformation.
Curved feather or leaf band with overlapping contours.
Curved two-strand braid. Its crossing cadence is relevant, but its centerline geometry is outside the straight-line scope.
Curved spiral pairs with curved enclosing turns. The small corner marks alone do not describe the full row.
Curved leaves alternating along a straight stem.
Curved scroll or paisley-like motifs. Their translated arrangement remains relevant for a later curve study.
